1.3.1.2-f73.text: Hinc metuunt, cupiuntque, dolent, fugiuntque, nec auras / Respiciunt clausi tenebris, & carcere caeco.

translations.note: Virgil, Aeneid 6.733–734, describes souls imprisoned in the body. The standard text reads 'dolent gaudentque, neque auras / dispiciunt clausae' (they grieve and rejoice, and do not see the air, shut in). Burton has 'fugiuntque' (and flee), 'nec ... respiciunt' (do not look back to) and the masculine 'clausi', which turns the line toward melancholy men. Burton's English verse leaves out 'desire'.

burton_span.exact: Hence ’tis they grieve and fear, avoiding light, / And shut themselves in prison dark from sight.

translations.text: Hence they fear and desire, they grieve and flee, and do not look back to the open air, / shut up in darkness and a blind prison.

burton_span.exact: That wandered in the woods sad all alone, / Forsaking men’s society, making great moan.

1.3.1.2-f74.text: Qui miser in sylvis maerens errabat opacis, / Ipse suum cor edens, hominum vestigia vitans.

translations.literal: Who wretched in woods grieving wandered shady, / himself his own heart eating, of men the footsteps avoiding.
translations.note: Homer, Iliad 6.201–202, on Bellerophon, in the Latin verse version Cicero gives (Tusculan Disputations 3.63): 'qui miser in campis maerens errabat Aleis' (in the Aleian plains). Burton has 'in sylvis ... opacis' (in the shadowy woods).
